pronunciation.approximation: FRAY-ur — the ey is a single falling diphthong (between the 'ay' of 'day' and the 'oy' of 'boy'), and the final -r is the nominative ending, lightly syllabic as in modern Icelandic Freyr.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Freyr descends from Proto-Germanic *frawjaz 'lord' — the same word as Gothic frauja and Old English frēa — and is the masculine counterpart of Freyja, from *frawjōn 'lady'. The ey is the Old Norse diphthong born from an earlier au, which is why a normalized Viking-Age carving reads ᚠᚱᛅᚢᛦ, frauR: the runes keep the older shape of the word. The normalized Old Norse form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no thorn or eth — so the name is Tier-2 by the mechanical rule: nothing distinctive is lost in transit, a statement about orthography, never about the god.

domains.title: The Lord (from *frawjaz) of the Peace-Years
domains.subtitle: Fertility, Sunshine, Rain
domains.lead: Freyr is the Vanir god the Æsir received in the hostage-exchange and never gave back: son of Njǫrðr, brother of Freyja, lord of Álfheimr, the ruler of rain and sunshine and the fruit of the earth — the god Snorri says it is good to call on for harvest and peace, and who governs the wealth of men.

cards.name: Gullinbursti
cards.desc: The golden-bristled boar the dwarfs Brokkr and Sindri forged, whose bristles light the night as it runs faster than any horse through air and water.

cards.name: Skíðblaðnir
cards.desc: The best of all ships, built by the sons of Ívaldi: fair wind whenever the sail is raised, room for all the Æsir armed — and it folds like cloth into a pouch.

cards.name: The Self-Wielding Sword
cards.desc: The sword that fights by itself for the wise — the price Freyr paid for Gerðr, and the blade he will miss when Surtr comes.

cards.name: Álfheimr
cards.desc: The realm of the elves, given to Freyr as a tooth-gift — a god's first present, and the seat of the lord of the shining world.

symbols.name: Gullinbursti
symbols.meaning: The golden-bristled boar whose glow turns night to day — the sun and the sowing made animal

symbols.name: Skíðblaðnir
symbols.meaning: The ship that always has a fair wind and folds into a pouch — prosperity that travels

symbols.name: The self-wielding sword
symbols.meaning: The weapon given away for love — the price of desire, paid at Ragnarök

symbols.name: The hart's antler
symbols.meaning: The improvised weapon of the swordless god — he killed Beli with one, and faces Surtr with none left

symbols.name: Álfheimr
symbols.meaning: The tooth-gift realm of the elves — light's homeland as a god's first possession

mythology.lead: Freyr's myths turn on a single economy: what the lord of plenty gives away. He gives Skírnir his sword for love of Gerðr, gives his peace-years to the Swedes, and gives his life at Ragnarök — swordless, facing the fire, because the price was paid long before.

myths.title: The Lord (from *frawjaz) of Harvest and Peace
myths.text: Snorri's portrait is the tradition's fixed formula: Freyr is the most glorious of the Æsir, son of Njǫrðr, and 'he rules over rain and sunshine, and therewith the fruit of the earth; it is good to call on him for harvest and peace — ár ok frið. He also governs the prosperity of men.' Grímnismál adds the deed that seats him: Álfheimr, the world of the elves, was given to Freyr by the gods in ancient days as a tooth-gift — the present made to a child when its first tooth comes. The Vanir hostage becomes the Æsir's own lord of the growing world.

myths.title: The Price of Gerðr
myths.text: Freyr had seated himself in Hliðskjálf, Óðinn's high seat that overlooks all worlds, and looked north into Jǫtunheimr — and saw a maiden walking from her father's hall to her bower, whose white arms lit the sky and the sea. From that sight he took a sickness of longing so deep he could neither sleep nor speak, and Njǫrðr sent his servant Skírnir to draw out what ailed him. Freyr confessed: Gerðr, daughter of the giant Gymir, had bound his heart, and no god and no elf would ever let them be together. Skírnir bargained for the errand: give me your sword — the one that fights by itself if he is wise who wields it — and your horse that will not shy at the magic flame. Freyr gave both, and rode nothing and carried nothing as Skírnir went over wet mountains to Gymir's courts, broke Gerðr's refusal by gifts, runes, and threats, and won her promise: nine nights hence, in the grove called Barri, she would grant Freyr her love. The poem ends on the waiting god's own arithmetic: 'Long is one night, longer is two — how shall I endure three?'

myths.title: The Gifts of the Dwarfs
myths.text: Two of the six treasures of the gods belong to Freyr. Skíðblaðnir, the best of ships, was made by the dwarfs called the sons of Ívaldi: large enough to carry all the Æsir with their weapons, always granted a fair wind the moment its sail is hoisted, and yet so cunningly built that it folds together like a cloth and goes into a pouch. Gullinbursti, the golden-bristled boar, was forged by Brokkr and Sindri in the same wager that made Mjǫllnir: it can run through air and water faster than any horse, and its bristles shine so brightly that night turns to day wherever it fares. When Baldr was burned, Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa — carved on an Icelandic hall's panels around 983 — remembered Freyr riding to the pyre on the boar; Snorri gives him a chariot drawn by Gullinbursti for the same journey.

myths.title: Swordless Against Surtr
myths.text: The Edda keeps the ledger. Lokasenna's Týr throws the bargain in Freyr's face: with gold you bought Gymir's daughter and sold your sword — when Muspell's sons ride through the dark wood, wretch, you will not know what to fight with. Gylfaginning recalls that Freyr once killed the giant Beli bare-handed, striking him down with a hart's antler, and could have slain him with his fist — but at Ragnarök improvisation runs out. When Surtr comes out of the south with fire, Freyr goes against him, and his death, Snorri says, comes the harder because he lacks the good sword he gave Skírnir. Vǫluspá's seeress watches it happen: the shining lord of the gods falls before the black one, and the earth sinks into the sea behind him. The god of the peace-years dies of the one gift he could not take back.

myths.title: The King Who Would Not Die
myths.text: Snorri's other Freyr is the euhemerized king of the Swedes. Freyr — also named Yngvi, whence the Ynglings took their name — succeeded Njǫrðr at Uppsala, built the great temple there, gathered all the wealth and land-rents of the realm into his own hand, and in his days began the Fróði-peace, the famous peace-years of good seasons and plenty, so that the Swedes credited their harvests to their king. He was so beloved that when he fell sick and died, his men would not burn him: they built him a great mound with three holes, told the people he lived, and for three years the Swedes poured the tribute — gold, silver, copper — down into the mound while the peace held. When at last the truth was known, the Swedes still refused to burn him; they called him the god of the world and sacrificed to him ever after for peace and good seasons. It is the clearest portrait the North kept of sacral kingship: the king as a weather-guarantee, worth more dead than any successor alive.

lore.syncretism: Freyr's name is a title, and titles travel. His Proto-Germanic *frawjaz 'lord' is the Gothic frauja — the very word Ulfilas uses for the Lord (from *frawjaz) in his Bible — and the Old English poetic frēa, 'lord' of kings and of God. His other name opens the oldest debate: Lokasenna calls him Ingunar-Freyr, Ynglingatal names the dynasty from Yngvi-Freyr, and scholars since Grimm have linked that Ing-element to the Inguaeones, the peoples Tacitus says descend from Mannus through Ing — the same Ing the Old English Rune Poem remembers as first seen among the East Danes before he went east over the wave. The equation Ing = Yngvi = Freyr is argued, not proven, and Simek counsels the usual caution; what is certain is the shape of the god: a lord whose name is 'Lord (from *frawjaz)', worshipped at the fountainhead of a royal line. Adam of Bremen gives the interpretatio from the outside: at Uppsala the Swedes called him Fricco, granted him peace and pleasure, and carved him ithyphallic between Thor and Wodan — a Germanic Priapus in a triad of his own.
lore.culturalLegacy: Freyr never left the North. His cult geography is written across the map in hundreds of Norwegian and Swedish place-names — Frøysland, Frøsvoll, Frösåker, Fröslunda — the densest theophoric landscape of any god after Þórr and Óðinn. The name itself survives as a living given name: Freyr in Iceland, Frej in Denmark and Sweden. His historical afterlife is the Yngling one: Norwegian and Swedish kings traced their lines through the Ynglings to Yngvi-Freyr, and Snorri's peace-years king became medieval Scandinavia's standing image of the good reign. Modern Heathenry keeps him at the centre of its harvest and fertility blóts under the old formula ár ok frið — harvest and peace — and the golden boar still runs through modern fantasy, games, and jewellery as the sun-animal of the Vanir.
lore.extendedMeditation: Freyr is the god who teaches what lordship costs. His name is not a name at all but the word 'Lord (from *frawjaz)' itself — every king, every master, every owner borrowing his title for as long as the peace holds. And the peace holds only by giving: the sword for the bride, the tribute for the mound, the life for the world. The Edda's arithmetic is merciless — the self-wielding sword is the one thing that cannot be given away and kept — but Freyr gives it anyway, and the tradition honours him not for the fight he loses at Ragnarök but for the peace-years he bought while he could. The lord of plenty is the god of the gift you cannot take back.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Freyr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚠᚱᛅᚢᛦ (f-r-a-u-R, ᛦ writing the final nominative -r), a form that keeps the older two-syllable frauR still close to *frawjaz 'lord'. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: freyr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Freyr is one of the few Norse gods with a plausible cult-image in the ground: the Rällinge statuette, a small seated Viking-Age bronze from Lunda in Södermanland, Sweden — cross-legged, bearded, and unmistakably ithyphallic — has been identified as Freyr since its discovery in 1904, and it matches Adam of Bremen's eyewitness description of Fricco at Uppsala with uncanny economy. Uppsala itself anchors the cult: Adam describes the great temple and its triad around 1075, and the royal mounds of Gamla Uppsala still stand where Ynglinga saga sets King Freyr's own mound. The theophoric place-name record — hundreds of Frøy-/Frö- names across Norway and Sweden, many compounded with 'grove', 'field', and 'meadow' — is the densest evidence of a working fertility cult. Against this, the runic corpus is silent: no inscription invokes the god by name, and the normalized Younger Futhark rendering ᚠᚱᛅᚢᛦ (frauR) is a reconstruction of how the name would have been carved. The literary witnesses are the Codex Regius (Skírnismál, Grímnismál, Lokasenna, Vǫluspá) and, for the carved-panel evidence, Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa (c. 983), preserved in Skáldskaparmál, which shows the boar-riding Freyr already a fixture of pre-Christian hall art.
